48226\\nCPF 3-2022-047-NOPV\\nDear Mr. Slater:\\nFrom August 23 to August 27, 2021, a representative of the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials\\nSafety Administration (PHMSA), Office of Pipeline Safety (OPS), pursuant to Chapter 601 of 49\\nUnited States Code (U.S.C.), inspected DTE Midstream Appalachia, LLC’s (DTM) Control\\nRoom Management procedures and records in Detroit, Michigan.\\nAs a result of the inspection, it is alleged that DTM has committed probable violations of the\\nPipeline Safety Regulations, Title 49, Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). The items inspected\\nand the probable violations are:\\n1.\\n\\n§ 192.631 Control room management.\\n(a) . . . .\\n(b) Roles and responsibilities. Each operator must define the roles and\\nresponsibilities of a controller during normal, abnormal and emergency operating\\nconditions. To provide for a controller’s prompt and appropriate response to\\noperating conditions, an operator must define each of the following: . . . .\\n\\n\\fDTE Midstream Appalachia’s (DTM) CRM Plan and Operator Qualification Plan were\\ninadequate because they allowed a 1:2 (1 qualified controller : 2 unqualified controllers) span of\\ncontrol during the on-the-job training (OJT) of controllers. 49 C.F.R. § 192.805(c) states an\\noperator's plan shall include provisions to \\\". . . . allow individuals that are not qualified pursuant\\nto this subpart to perform a covered task if directed and observed by an individual that is\\nqualified.\\\" The critical words here being “directed and observed.” DTM’s 1:2 span of control\\ndid not provide conditions where the senior controller (qualified trainer) was free and available\\nto monitor the controller to direct and observe their actions and be ready to respond to, and\\naddress, situations that might arise. This is because the unqualified controller trainee was\\nindependently monitoring and controlling their own console while the qualified controller trainer\\nwas operating a separate console. This practice is not appropriate for the safe operation of a\\npipeline system.\\nA review of various shift schedules provided by DTM from 2019 and 2021, identified 40\\ndifferent days where unqualified controllers were operating the DTE Midstream Appalachian\\nBirdsboro Pipeline on the Blue Stone (BSP) console independently while the senior controller\\nwas operating a separate console in the DTE Detroit (DTE) control room. Of these 40 days, 4\\ndays identified that two unqualified controllers were operating under one senior controller, all on\\ndifferent consoles. Of the other 36 days, two or more senior controllers were on shift operating\\nseparate consoles with the unqualified controllers.\\nDTM’s CRM Plan defined a Non-Qualified Gas Controller as “[A]n individual that performs all\\nthe same actions as a Senior or Principal Gas Control under the Senior or Principal Gas\\nController’s guidance and direction”. A Qualified Gas Controller was defined as “[A]n\\nindividual that has been evaluated and can perform assigned Covered Tasks and recognize and\\nreact to Abnormal Operating Conditions (AOC) without the guidance and direction of a Senior\\nor Principal Gas Controller”. With the Senior Controller operating his/her own system(s), it is\\nnot realistic to direct, observe or guide the unqualified trainee to support the safe operation of the\\npipeline. A review of Figure 1: Main Control Room Layout in the CRM Plan identified that\\ncontroller consoles were spaced too far apart and that the qualified controllers would not be able\\nto recognize and direct/react to abnormal operations that may arise on another console. If the\\nSenior Controller is attentive to his/her console, then he/she cannot be attentive to the\\nunqualified controller’s console.\\nThe concept of span of control, when considering controller OJT training, must consider that the\\nqualified controller is the one responsible and accountable for monitoring and controlling a\\nconsole and the systems related to that console. Through their observation of the system, via\\nSCADA, and the observation of the trainee’s actions, the qualified controller recognizes and\\ndirects the actions of the controller. While the trainee is the one sending set points, opening\\nvalves, and responding to alarms, they are making these changes with the permission of, and by\\nthe direction of, the qualified controller through direct observation.\\nThe operator’s 1:2 span of control, combined with their practice of the trainer (senior controller)\\nmonitoring and controlling their own console, in addition to up to 2 controller trainees who are\\nalso independently operating their own systems, means that the senior controller is operating a\\ntotal of 2 to 3 separate consoles which is not conducive for the safe operation of the pipeline.\\n\\n2\\n\\n\\fAdditionally, ASME B31Q is a standard available to operators to guide them when considering\\ntask development and span of control. B31Q, Task 1371 Operate Gas Pipeline - System Control\\nCenter Operations suggests a span of control as 1:1. There is also a rating for importance and\\ndifficulty of the task of 4 and 5, respectively. For comparison, if one considers tasks that are\\nrecommended 1:2 span of control, these include typical difficulty and importance ratings of 3\\nand 4 respectively. Examples of tasks with 1:2 span of control include Tasks 0321 Valve\\nCorrective Maintenance, 0481 Centrifugal Compressor Inspection, Testing and Maintenance and\\n0581 Pressure Test: Liquid Medium.\\nA review of the shift schedules verified that the unqualified controller trainees were not assigned\\nto a specific trainer for any length of time. Additionally, while one or more senior controller(s)\\nwas assigned to a shift, the trainee did not have the same person as the trainer for more than 3 or\\n4 days in a row. With DTE’s practice of unstructured and undocumented OJT training, it would\\nbe difficult for a trainer to know where a trainee was in their knowledge and skill of pipeline\\noperations. There was no training log to communicate the trainee’s status and competencies/\\ndeficiencies between the senior controllers overseeing the unqualified controller trainee. This\\nconsole rotational practice emphasizes the need for a 1:1 span of control.\\n2.\\n\\n§ 192.631 Control room management.\\n(a) . . . .\\n(c) Provide adequate information. Each operator must provide its controllers with\\nthe information, tools, processes and procedures necessary for the controllers to\\ncarry out the roles and responsibilities the operator has defined by performing each\\nof the following:\\n(1) Implement sections 1, 4, 8, 9, 11.1, 11.3 of API RP 1165 (incorporated by\\nreference, see § 192.7) whenever a SCADA system is added, expanded or replaced,\\nunless the operator demonstrates that certain provisions of sections 1, 4, 8, 9, 11.1,\\n11.3 of API RP 1165 are not practical for the SCADA system used;\\n\\nDTM failed to verify that sections of API RP 1165 provided in § 192.631(c)(1) were\\nimplemented in their SCADA system. DTM indicated they developed the SCADA Style Guide\\nto meet the prescribed requirements of API 1165 and the SCADA screens were designed from\\nthe Style Guide requirements. DTM has not performed an audit or documented comparison of\\ntheir SCADA Style Guide to verify the SCADA system and screens perform as required by the\\nprescribed sections of API 1165, per its Style Guide.\\n\\n3\\n\\n\\f3.\\n\\n§ 192.631 Control room management.\\n(a) . . . .\\n(e) Alarm management. Each operator using a SCADA system must have a written\\nalarm management plan to provide for effective controller response to alarms. An\\noperator’s plan must include provisions to:\\n(1) Review SCADA safety-related alarm operations using a process that ensures\\nalarms are accurate and support safe pipeline operations;\\n\\nDTM failed to implement, in their SCADA system, designations of safety-related alarms that\\nwere readily available to the controller, and supported effective controller response to alarms for\\nsafe operations of the pipeline. At the time of the inspection, procedures were inadequate\\nbecause they did not provide guidance for effective controller response to alarms. DTM supports\\nmany procedures related to how to address specific alarms, but it did not have one related to\\ngeneral alarm handling. MAIL TO: trusso@buckeye.com\\nFebruary 13, 2026\\nMr. Todd Russo\\nPresident & Chief Executive Officer\\nBuckeye Partners, LP\\n4200 Westheimer Road, Suite 975\\nHouston, Texas 77027\\nCPF 1-2026-003-NOPV\\nDear Mr. Russo:\\nFrom June 4 through December 3, 2024, a representative of the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials\\nSafety Administration (PHMSA) pursuant to Chapter 601 of 49 United States Code (U.S.C.)\\ninspected Buckeye Partners, LP’s (Buckeye) construction records and observed excavation of\\nTampa Pipelines L931 and L932 as part of a weld validation and testing plan in Allentown,\\nPennsylvania, and Tampa, Florida.\\nAs a result of the inspection, it is alleged that you have committed probable violations of the\\nPipeline Safety Regulations, Title 49, Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). The items inspected\\nand the probable violations are:\\n1.\\n\\n§ 195.202 Compliance with specifications or standards\\nEach pipeline system must be constructed in accordance with comprehensive\\nwritten specifications or standards that are consistent with the requirements of this\\npart.\\n\\nBuckeye failed to construct its pipeline system in accordance with comprehensive written\\nspecifications or standards that are consistent with the requirements of 49 CFR Part 195 in\\naccordance with section 195.202. Specifically, Buckeye failed to document coating system\\nselection, handling and storage, application, inspection, and repair data, as required by its\\n\\n\\fCPF 1-2026-003-NOPV\\nConstruction Specification CS-PL-002, Coating Below Grade Piping Systems, Rev-3\\n(06/22/2017) (Coating Specification), section 14.\\nSection 14.1.1 of Buckeye’s Coating Specification stated that coating system selection, handling\\nand storage, application, inspection, and repair data required by this procedure will be documented\\nby the company corrosion control personnel, Project Manager, or their designee, and that the\\ncoating data is maintained for the life of the system.\\nSection 14.1.2 of Buckeye’s Coating Specification stated that readings and recordings for newly\\nconstructed assets should be documented on the form CF-PL-0002, Field Installed Below Grade\\nCoating Test Record (CF-PL-002). CF-PL-002 included information regarding ambient\\nconditions, surface preparation, coating application and product used, dry film thickness (DFT)\\nreadings, and coating inspection and repairs.\\nHowever, when PHMSA requested records pertaining to the application, inspection, and repair of\\nbelow grade coating applied during the construction of the Tampa Pipelines L931 and L932,\\nBuckeye failed to provide any completed CF-PL-0002 forms, thus failing to maintain, for at least\\n5 years, a record of each inspection required by 49 CFR Part 195 Subpart H in sufficient detail to\\ndemonstrate the adequacy of corrosion control measures in accordance with section 195.589(c).\\nTherefore, Buckeye failed to construct its pipeline system in accordance with comprehensive\\nwritten specifications or standards that are consistent with the requirements of 49 CFR Part 195\\nin accordance with section 195.202.\\n2.\\n\\n§ 195.202 Compliance with specifications or standards.\\nEach pipeline system must be constructed in accordance with\\ncomprehensive written specifications or standards that are consistent\\nwith the requirements of this part.\\n\\nBuckeye failed to construct its pipeline system in accordance with comprehensive written\\nspecifications or standards that are consistent with the requirements of 49 CFR Part 195 in\\naccordance with section 195.202. Specifically, Buckeye failed to properly prepare the surface\\nprior to coating, and apply, and inspect the coating material, as required by Denso Protal 7200\\nBrush Application Specifications (Denso Application Specification) and its Construction\\nSpecification CS-PL-002, Coating Below Grade Piping Systems, Rev-3 (06/22/2017) (Coating\\nSpecification), section 10.\\nDuring the pipeline field inspection, PHMSA observed peeled and disbonded field-applied coating\\nalong several locations of the Tampa Pipelines L931 and L932. The coating, applied in the field\\nto protect pipeline girth welds and to repair pipe coating defects, was Denso Protal 7200 (which is\\na two-part epoxy product). 1 The prevalence of the coating deficiencies indicated poor coating\\nadhesion, most likely caused by improper surface preparation and coating application during\\nconstruction. The lack of coating adhesion caused by improper surface preparation allows\\n1\\n\\nThe pipe was exposed as part of ongoing excavation within its right-of-way to address construction deficiencies that\\nwere previously found by PHMSA. See Notice of Probable Violation and Proposed Compliance Order, CPF No. 12025-001-NOPV.\\n\\nPage 2 of 7\\n\\n\\fCPF 1-2026-003-NOPV\\nmoisture to collect between the coating and the steel pipeline surface and creates the potential for\\nexternal corrosion and metal loss.\\nSection 4 of Denso Application Specification states in part that all contaminants shall be removed\\nfrom the steel surface to be coated, and that oil and grease should be removed in accordance with\\nthe surface preparation standard SSPC SP-1 using non-oily solvent cleaner. It also states that all\\nsurfaces to be coated shall be abrasive blasted to a near-white finish and it indicates additional\\nrequirements as part of the surface preparation.\\nSection 10.1.1 of Buckeye’s Coating Specification required that, prior to coating, Buckeye must\\nensure the exposed surface is free of moisture, dust, dirt, oil, grease, weld, splatter, slag or other\\ncontaminants which might interfere with the coating or adhesion of the coating to the metal or\\nadjacent coating unless otherwise allowed by coating manufacturer instructions. Sections 10.2\\nand 10.3 stated that abrasive blasting or power tools may be used to generate surface profile\\nrequirements. Section 10.4 required Buckeye to inspect the prepped surface and record the relative\\nhumidity, ambient temperature, dew point temperature, and surface temperature prior to coating.\\nPHMSA requested records and any other information available related to the surface preparation,\\napplication, and inspection of the field-applied coating. However, Buckeye failed to provide\\nevidence that it prepared, applied, and inspected the coating material as required by its Coating\\nSpecification.\\nInstead, Buckeye provided “DOT Mill Readings,” 2 with dry film thickness (DFT) readings dated\\nfrom 12/04/2018 to 8/11/2020 and photos 3 depicting a technician applying coating to two girth\\nwelds, 4 attaining a DFT reading, and inspecting 12-inch diameter pipe joints with mill-applied\\nFusion Bonded Epoxy (FBE) coating utilizing a coating discontinuity or “holiday” detector. 5 The\\nDOT Mill Readings included a coating product name (Protal 7200), and detector voltage\\nsettings/readings, however these records did not include the relative humidity, ambient\\ntemperature, dew point temperature, and surface temperature prior to coating, or include any other\\ninformation related to surface preparation, and the results of any visual inspection before or after\\ncoating application. Moreover, these records failed to include the results of the holiday inspection\\nand note if any defects were remediated prior to installation of the pipe. 1-2026-003-NOPV\\nDear Mr. Russo:\\nFrom June 4 through December 3, 2024, a representative of the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials\\nSafety Administration (PHMSA) pursuant to Chapter 601 of 49 United States Code (U.S.C.)\\ninspected Buckeye Partners, LP’s (Buckeye) construction records and observed excavation of\\nTampa Pipelines L931 and L932 as part of a weld validation and testing plan in Allentown,\\nPennsylvania, and Tampa, Florida.\\nAs a result of the inspection, it is alleged that you have committed probable violations of the\\nPipeline Safety Regulations, Title 49, Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). The items inspected\\nand the probable violations are:\\n1.\\n\\n§ 195.202 Compliance with specifications or standards\\nEach pipeline system must be constructed in accordance with comprehensive\\nwritten specifications or standards that are consistent with the requirements of this\\npart.\\n\\nBuckeye failed to construct its pipeline system in accordance with comprehensive written\\nspecifications or standards that are consistent with the requirements of 49 CFR Part 195 in\\naccordance with section 195.202. Specifically, Buckeye failed to document coating system\\nselection, handling and storage, application, inspection, and repair data, as required by its\\n\\n\\fCPF 1-2026-003-NOPV\\nConstruction Specification CS-PL-002, Coating Below Grade Piping Systems, Rev-3\\n(06/22/2017) (Coating Specification), section 14.\\nSection 14.1.1 of Buckeye’s Coating Specification stated that coating system selection, handling\\nand storage, application, inspection, and repair data required by this procedure will be documented\\nby the company corrosion control personnel, Project Manager, or their designee, and that the\\ncoating data is maintained for the life of the system.\\nSection 14.1.2 of Buckeye’s Coating Specification stated that readings and recordings for newly\\nconstructed assets should be documented on the form CF-PL-0002, Field Installed Below Grade\\nCoating Test Record (CF-PL-002). CF-PL-002 included information regarding ambient\\nconditions, surface preparation, coating application and product used, dry film thickness (DFT)\\nreadings, and coating inspection and repairs.\\nHowever, when PHMSA requested records pertaining to the application, inspection, and repair of\\nbelow grade coating applied during the construction of the Tampa Pipelines L931 and L932,\\nBuckeye failed to provide any completed CF-PL-0002 forms, thus failing to maintain, for at least\\n5 years, a record of each inspection required by 49 CFR Part 195 Subpart H in sufficient detail to\\ndemonstrate the adequacy of corrosion control measures in accordance with section 195.589(c).\\nTherefore, Buckeye failed to construct its pipeline system in accordance with comprehensive\\nwritten specifications or standards that are consistent with the requirements of 49 CFR Part 195\\nin accordance with section 195.202.\\n2.\\n\\n§ 195.202 Compliance with specifications or standards.\\nEach pipeline system must be constructed in accordance with\\ncomprehensive written specifications or standards that are consistent\\nwith the requirements of this part.\\n\\nBuckeye failed to construct its pipeline system in accordance with comprehensive written\\nspecifications or standards that are consistent with the requirements of 49 CFR Part 195 in\\naccordance with section 195.202. Specifically, Buckeye failed to properly prepare the surface\\nprior to coating, and apply, and inspect the coating material, as required by Denso Protal 7200\\nBrush Application Specifications (Denso Application Specification) and its Construction\\nSpecification CS-PL-002, Coating Below Grade Piping Systems, Rev-3 (06/22/2017) (Coating\\nSpecification), section 10.\\nDuring the pipeline field inspection, PHMSA observed peeled and disbonded field-applied coating\\nalong several locations of the Tampa Pipelines L931 and L932. The coating, applied in the field\\nto protect pipeline girth welds and to repair pipe coating defects, was Denso Protal 7200 (which is\\na two-part epoxy product). 1 The prevalence of the coating deficiencies indicated poor coating\\nadhesion, most likely caused by improper surface preparation and coating application during\\nconstruction. The lack of coating adhesion caused by improper surface preparation allows\\n1\\n\\nThe pipe was exposed as part of ongoing excavation within its right-of-way to address construction deficiencies that\\nwere previously found by PHMSA. See Notice of Probable Violation and Proposed Compliance Order, CPF No. 12025-001-NOPV.\\n\\nPage 2 of 7\\n\\n\\fCPF 1-2026-003-NOPV\\nmoisture to collect between the coating and the steel pipeline surface and creates the potential for\\nexternal corrosion and metal loss.\\nSection 4 of Denso Application Specification states in part that all contaminants shall be removed\\nfrom the steel surface to be coated, and that oil and grease should be removed in accordance with\\nthe surface preparation standard SSPC SP-1 using non-oily solvent cleaner. It also states that all\\nsurfaces to be coated shall be abrasive blasted to a near-white finish and it indicates additional\\nrequirements as part of the surface preparation.\\nSection 10.1.1 of Buckeye’s Coating Specification required that, prior to coating, Buckeye must\\nensure the exposed surface is free of moisture, dust, dirt, oil, grease, weld, splatter, slag or other\\ncontaminants which might interfere with the coating or adhesion of the coating to the metal or\\nadjacent coating unless otherwise allowed by coating manufacturer instructions. 1-2026-003-NOPV\\nDear Mr. Russo:\\nFrom June 4 through December 3, 2024, a representative of the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials\\nSafety Administration (PHMSA) pursuant to Chapter 601 of 49 United States Code (U.S.C.)\\ninspected Buckeye Partners, LP’s (Buckeye) construction records and observed excavation of\\nTampa Pipelines L931 and L932 as part of a weld validation and testing plan in Allentown,\\nPennsylvania, and Tampa, Florida.\\nAs a result of the inspection, it is alleged that you have committed probable violations of the\\nPipeline Safety Regulations, Title 49, Code of Federal Regulations (CFR). The items inspected\\nand the probable violations are:\\n1.\\n\\n§ 195.202 Compliance with specifications or standards\\nEach pipeline system must be constructed in accordance with comprehensive\\nwritten specifications or standards that are consistent with the requirements of this\\npart.\\n\\nBuckeye failed to construct its pipeline system in accordance with comprehensive written\\nspecifications or standards that are consistent with the requirements of 49 CFR Part 195 in\\naccordance with section 195.202. Specifically, Buckeye failed to document coating system\\nselection, handling and storage, application, inspection, and repair data, as required by its\\n\\n\\fCPF 1-2026-003-NOPV\\nConstruction Specification CS-PL-002, Coating Below Grade Piping Systems, Rev-3\\n(06/22/2017) (Coating Specification), section 14.\\nSection 14.1.1 of Buckeye’s Coating Specification stated that coating system selection, handling\\nand storage, application, inspection, and repair data required by this procedure will be documented\\nby the company corrosion control personnel, Project Manager, or their designee, and that the\\ncoating data is maintained for the life of the system.\\nSection 14.1.2 of Buckeye’s Coating Specification stated that readings and recordings for newly\\nconstructed assets should be documented on the form CF-PL-0002, Field Installed Below Grade\\nCoating Test Record (CF-PL-002). CF-PL-002 included information regarding ambient\\nconditions, surface preparation, coating application and product used, dry film thickness (DFT)\\nreadings, and coating inspection and repairs.\\nHowever, when PHMSA requested records pertaining to the application, inspection, and repair of\\nbelow grade coating applied during the construction of the Tampa Pipelines L931 and L932,\\nBuckeye failed to provide any completed CF-PL-0002 forms, thus failing to maintain, for at least\\n5 years, a record of each inspection required by 49 CFR Part 195 Subpart H in sufficient detail to\\ndemonstrate the adequacy of corrosion control measures in accordance with section 195.589(c).\\nTherefore, Buckeye failed to construct its pipeline system in accordance with comprehensive\\nwritten specifications or standards that are consistent with the requirements of 49 CFR Part 195\\nin accordance with section 195.202.\\n2.\\n\\n§ 195.202 Compliance with specifications or standards.\\nEach pipeline system must be constructed in accordance with\\ncomprehensive written specifications or standards that are consistent\\nwith the requirements of this part.\\n\\nBuckeye failed to construct its pipeline system in accordance with comprehensive written\\nspecifications or standards that are consistent with the requirements of 49 CFR Part 195 in\\naccordance with section 195.202. Specifically, Buckeye failed to properly prepare the surface\\nprior to coating, and apply, and inspect the coating material, as required by Denso Protal 7200\\nBrush Application Specifications (Denso Application Specification) and its Construction\\nSpecification CS-PL-002, Coating Below Grade Piping Systems, Rev-3 (06/22/2017) (Coating\\nSpecification), section 10.\\nDuring the pipeline field inspection, PHMSA observed peeled and disbonded field-applied coating\\nalong several locations of the Tampa Pipelines L931 and L932. The coating, applied in the field\\nto protect pipeline girth welds and to repair pipe coating defects, was Denso Protal 7200 (which is\\na two-part epoxy product). 1 The prevalence of the coating deficiencies indicated poor coating\\nadhesion, most likely caused by improper surface preparation and coating application during\\nconstruction. The lack of coating adhesion caused by improper surface preparation allows\\n1\\n\\nThe pipe was exposed as part of ongoing excavation within its right-of-way to address construction deficiencies that\\nwere previously found by PHMSA. See Notice of Probable Violation and Proposed Compliance Order, CPF No. 12025-001-NOPV.\\n\\nPage 2 of 7\\n\\n\\fCPF 1-2026-003-NOPV\\nmoisture to collect between the coating and the steel pipeline surface and creates the potential for\\nexternal corrosion and metal loss.\\nSection 4 of Denso Application Specification states in part that all contaminants shall be removed\\nfrom the steel surface to be coated, and that oil and grease should be removed in accordance with\\nthe surface preparation standard SSPC SP-1 using non-oily solvent cleaner. It also states that all\\nsurfaces to be coated shall be abrasive blasted to a near-white finish and it indicates additional\\nrequirements as part of the surface preparation.\\nSection 10.1.1 of Buckeye’s Coating Specification required that, prior to coating, Buckeye must\\nensure the exposed surface is free of moisture, dust, dirt, oil, grease, weld, splatter, slag or other\\ncontaminants which might interfere with the coating or adhesion of the coating to the metal or\\nadjacent coating unless otherwise allowed by coating manufacturer instructions. Sections 10.2\\nand 10.3 stated that abrasive blasting or power tools may be used to generate surface profile\\nrequirements. Section 10.4 required Buckeye to inspect the prepped surface and record the relative\\nhumidity, ambient temperature, dew point temperature, and surface temperature prior to coating.\\nPHMSA requested records and any other information available related to the surface preparation,\\napplication, and inspection of the field-applied coating. However, Buckeye failed to provide\\nevidence that it prepared, applied, and inspected the coating material as required by its Coating\\nSpecification.\\nInstead, Buckeye provided “DOT Mill Readings,” 2 with dry film thickness (DFT) readings dated\\nfrom 12/04/2018 to 8/11/2020 and photos 3 depicting a technician applying coating to two girth\\nwelds, 4 attaining a DFT reading, and inspecting 12-inch diameter pipe joints with mill-applied\\nFusion Bonded Epoxy (FBE) coating utilizing a coating discontinuity or “holiday” detector. 5 The\\nDOT Mill Readings included a coating product name (Protal 7200), and detector voltage\\nsettings/readings, however these records did not include the relative humidity, ambient\\ntemperature, dew point temperature, and surface temperature prior to coating, or include any other\\ninformation related to surface preparation, and the results of any visual inspection before or after\\ncoating application. Moreover, these records failed to include the results of the holiday inspection\\nand note if any defects were remediated prior to installation of the pipe. Buckeye was unable to\\nprovide any other evidence of proper surface preparation, coating application, and associated\\ninspections.\\n\\n2\\n\\nSee Pipeline Safety Violation Report, Exhibit B-16, DOT Mill Readings Underground.\\n\\n3\\n\\nSee Pipeline Safety Violation Report, Exhibit B-17, Data Request E Tampa Field Weld Coating Process PhotosButane Site.\\n4\\n\\nTampa Pipelines L391 and L392 had over 300 girth welds with field-applied coating.\\n\\n5\\n\\nAs defined in NACE SP0169-2007 (Section 2), Holiday is a discontinuity in a protective coating that exposes\\nunprotected surface to the environment. A coating holiday detector is a specialized instrument used to identify\\ndiscontinuities, such as pinholes, cracks, or voids, in protective coatings applied to conductive or
